title: Obeying Incentives Is for Losers: You Should Decide Right and Wrong for Yourself
dek: Economists say fix the incentives and you fix the world. Mastroianni says that misses half of it: even if you have a reason to do wrong, you still shouldn't do it. Outsourcing your value judgments to an incentive structure is abandoning the core task of being a person.
why: Medium information density; the early stretch gets tangled up in Omelas and Rube Goldberg, and the real stuff is the big fish, Sumner, and high pay selecting the wrong people in the middle and back half.
who: For founders, investors and managers who depend professionally on incentive mechanisms — especially anyone designing team behavior with bonuses and titles.
skip: The literary discussion of Omelas from 3 to 12 minutes can be fast-forwarded; jump straight to the big fish at 20:33.

points.h: Having a reason to do wrong doesn't mean you should
points.body: Mastroianni first grants that incentive analysis beats ‘people are bad, so they do bad things’: at least it admits people have reasons, and changing the reasons might change the behavior. But he adds a premise economists often miss — if you do it because an external reward structure tells you it's good, because it will give you a pat on the head or a little treat, that's loser behavior. His exact words: even if you have a reason to do a bad thing, you still shouldn't do it. He jokes that this is an obvious point, but some points are so obvious that no one thinks to say them.

points.h: The real Omelas is a Rube Goldberg machine
points.body: In Le Guin's Omelas, the whole city's happiness rests on a tortured child in the basement, and some people choose to walk away. Mastroianni says that story was in his head when he wrote the piece, but he cut a section: in the story you have some metaphysical connection to the child, whereas in reality the connection is more like a Rube Goldberg machine — you're not the one torturing the child, you're three warehouses away, just the hammer that swings down, hits the ball, the ball rolls down the slope, lights the match. The bad thing is far from you, you didn't do it with your own hands, but you're in the causal chain. That makes ‘walking away’ much harder and far less heroic: it doesn't look like brushing the dust of Omelas off your feet, it looks like ‘I'm not going to be VP of brand partnerships for Philip Morris.’

points.h: Outsourcing value judgment means being conscripted by bad people
points.body: Russ asks: are you saying we should encourage people to be more moral? Mastroianni says he doesn't think this can be centrally organized, mandated, compelled or cultivated by government — when governments try, it tends to go bad fast. His goal is to produce the kind of person who does the right thing even when it's inconvenient, even when it's costly. He offers a chain: if you only do what's rewarded, you can start out amoral and end up deputized for the immoral. His judgment: bad people are rare; what's plentiful is people without a strong sense of right and wrong, and those people can be turned into an army by bad people.

points.h: The big fish will find you; you decide whether to look
points.body: The ‘big fish’ comes from Lovecraft's Dagon: a man sees a fish god, is never right again for the rest of his life, and finally jumps out a window. Mastroianni uses it as a metaphor — everyone has a fish inside them, and if you really take it seriously you have to overturn your entire life. His own fish was the 2020 Society for Personality and Social Psychology conference in San Francisco: the venue was in the Tenderloin, and inside people ate canapés and talked about reducing implicit bias by a tiny amount, possibly just noise, while outside people curled up with fentanyl in their veins. He specifically brings up the 1970s seminary student experiment: randomly assigned to speak on the Good Samaritan or on career opportunities, then randomly told they were late or on time, and the only thing that determined whether they stopped for the man lying by the road was whether they were in a hurry. He says this is one of the most famous findings in the field, everyone in that room knew it, and no one felt any conflict about it — that was the fish he saw.

points.h: Sumner went back to provoking after being caned
points.body: Charles Sumner is the man whose statue Mastroianni walked past every day in grad school. He came from a poor Boston family, his father was illegitimate; the place where he grew up was home to large numbers of formerly enslaved people. He went to France, and at the Sorbonne he saw Black and white students studying together as equals, and wrote in his diary: the difference between people is obviously not caused by nature, it can only be caused by education. He became a radical abolitionist, arguing not just for abolition but for racially integrated schools and Black suffrage — things that only became common sense more than a century later. As a senator he gave a fierce anti-slavery speech, and days later a Southern congressman walked up to his desk and beat him with a cane until he was nearly dead, trapped in his desk, soaking in his own blood, and it took him more than a year to recover. After recovering he went on being a provocateur, and he pushed Lincoln to issue the Emancipation Proclamation two years early. His new biographer says Sumner is cited 40 times in the brief for Brown v. Board.

points.h: Desperate to join the club of people you don't respect
points.body: Russ quotes Adam Smith: we want to be loved and to be lovely, so we should surround ourselves with good people whose approval we want. Mastroianni goes harder: he and the people close to him have spent their whole lives desperately seeking opportunities from people they don't respect, landing in an absurd position — ‘I think they're bad people, I think they're completely wrong about what's good and bad, but I really want them to let me into their club.’ Into it for what? You will inevitably become more like them, and you can't control it. He says the moment you can say ‘I distrust this person's judgment so much that even though he could give me success, I'll go do something else’ — that's the moment of freedom he described earlier: that person has no power over you anymore.

points.h: High pay doesn't buy you better professors
points.body: Russ says his own salary when he graduated was about $18,600 a year, and he's glad he didn't go into finance or a chief economist's office at a big company. He asks: economics professors can make $500,000 or even $750,000 a year — with more money, is it harder to maintain the norms of honesty and truth-seeking that founded the discipline? Mastroianni says this looks more like a selection effect than a corruption effect: the people attracted by $750,000 are often not the people who can be good professors; the consequence of high pay isn't corrupting people who might have been good, it's attracting people who shouldn't be there and making them compete with each other. Russ presses: doesn't paying $750,000 mean you should get the best professors? Mastroianni answers: the professor you want is someone who puts truth above everything, and once the money is big enough, the people who come are the ones who don't put truth first — and our selection procedures can't tell who's in it for truth and who's in it for the salary, especially since many of the people doing the selecting came for the wrong reasons themselves.

points.h: Status is harder to separate from knowledge than money is
points.body: Mastroianni says that in most places it isn't money that attracts the wrong people, it's status: being called professor feels good, so many people want it and so few get it. And status markers are harder to distinguish from knowledge markers than money markers are, because they claim to be knowledge markers themselves — ‘you published in a good journal, so it must be good work.’ He says we've now reached the point where people talk about writing a specific paper for a specific journal, and call papers pubs or A-pubs, and he finds it vile and disgusting, like defacing a cross. He says this is why he isn't in academia: he's willing to earn less to study what he thinks matters, to tolerate job insecurity, to move all over the world — but if after all that it's still ‘why don't you publish a pile of garbage papers’ and ‘why don't you massage the statistics a little,’ then it isn't worth it.

Mastroianni's metaphor: an unexamined belief that, once you face it squarely, forces you to overturn your entire life.
